title: Graphs and Topological Sort
summary: Model items and their relationships as nodes and edges, then traverse them to find order, reachability, or cycles.
lesson:
How it works
- A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges, which may be directed or undirected.
- An adjacency list maps each node to its neighbors and uses `O(V + E)` space.
- Breadth-first search (BFS) visits nodes in layers using a queue; depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as far as it goes using recursion or a stack. Both take `O(V + E)` time.

When to reach for it
- The input describes dependencies, prerequisites, connections, or grids of neighboring cells.
- The question asks whether something is reachable, what order satisfies all dependencies, or whether a cycle exists.
- You need shortest paths in an unweighted graph, which BFS gives directly.

Common patterns
- Topological sort with in-degrees: repeatedly take a node with no remaining incoming edges.
- Cycle detection in a directed graph: DFS with three states (unvisited, in progress, done).
- Connected components: run a traversal from every unvisited node.

Pitfalls
- Forgetting to mark nodes as visited, which loops forever on cycles.
- Recursion depth: deep DFS can overflow the stack; an explicit stack or BFS avoids it.
- Edge direction: "a depends on b" is an edge from `b` to `a` when you want a processing order.
- Nodes with no edges still count; include them in the traversal.
